title: Why and how to shard
summary: Shard for write throughput, storage and blast radius, not for reads. Pick the partition key from the access patterns, choose hash, range or a directory, and spot the hot shard before it pages you.

steps.title: One database is not enough (eventually)
body: **Sharding** splits one logical table across several databases. Each **shard** holds a slice of the rows and
has its own primary, replicas, disk and CPU. It is the last scaling step, not the first. Try these first:
| Pain | Cheaper fix first |
| Too many **reads** | a cache, read replicas, better indexes |
| Slow queries | an index, a smaller result, fewer round trips |
| CPU at 80% on a small box | a bigger box (vertical scaling goes a long way in 2026) |
Shard when one primary cannot keep up and nothing else helps:
- **Write throughput**: every write goes to the one primary. Replicas do not share that work.
- **Storage**: the data set outgrows one machine's disks, or backups and restores take too long.
- **Blast radius**: a bad migration or a runaway query hurts one shard's users, not everyone.
The bill: queries that span shards, transactions that span shards, uneven load, resharding later, and more
machines to run. A senior says *why not yet* as often as *how*.

steps.prompt: Which situation is the **weakest** reason to shard right now?
options: The product page is read 40,000 times a second; writes are 200 a second and the primary's CPU is at 35%
The primary takes 9,000 writes a second, is at 85% CPU on the largest instance size, and writes grow 10% a month
The table is 60 TB and a full restore takes two days, longer than the recovery time objective
One tenant's batch job slows every other tenant down, and contracts promise isolation
steps.explain: Read-heavy load with an idle primary is a job for a cache and read replicas. Sharding helps writes, storage and isolation; it does nothing a replica could not do for reads, at a much higher cost.

steps.title: The partition key, and three ways to split
body: The **partition key** decides which shard owns a row. Choose it from the **access patterns**: the most common
queries should touch one shard. For a shop, "show my orders" runs far more than "all orders on Tuesday", so
`customer_id` beats `order_date`.
| Scheme | How | Good at | Bad at |
| **Hash** | `shard = hash(key) mod N` (or a ring, next lesson) | spreading load evenly | range scans (`WHERE created BETWEEN ...` hits every shard) |
| **Range** | shard 0 holds keys `[0, 25M)`, shard 1 `[25M, 50M)`... | range scans, time-ordered data | hot spots when new keys all land at one end |
| **Directory** | a lookup table maps key (or tenant) to shard | moving one big tenant, uneven tenants | one more lookup, and the directory must be highly available |
```text
hash(customer_id) mod 4         range on created_at              directory
c17 -> s1   c18 -> s3          Jan -> s0   Feb -> s1            acme    -> s2
c19 -> s0   c20 -> s1          Mar -> s2   Apr -> s3  <- hot    globex  -> s0
- **Partition key**: the column that decides which shard owns a row; pick it so common queries hit one shard.

steps.prompt: Pick the partitioning scheme that fits each workload best.
items: User profiles, always read and written by `user_id`
Sensor readings queried as "last 24 hours for this sensor", keyed by `(sensor_id, time)`
B2B SaaS where three tenants are 100x bigger than the rest and must be movable on their own
Shopping carts keyed by `cart_id`, no range queries
An archive where old months move to cheaper shards
Regulated tenants that must live in a named region
steps.explain: Hash for even load on point lookups; range when queries scan ordered keys; a directory when you need to place specific keys (tenants) by hand.

steps.title: Hot spots, and salting the celebrity
body: Sharding only helps if load is **spread**. Two classic ways it is not:
1. **Time-ordered keys on range partitions.** Auto-increment ids, timestamps and UUIDv7 all grow. Every new
row lands on the last range, so one shard takes 100% of the inserts while the others sit idle.
2. **Celebrity keys.** Hashing spreads *keys*, not *traffic*. If one key (a famous account, a viral post) takes
30% of the writes, the shard that owns it takes 30% plus its fair share.
**Salting** spreads one hot key over several rows: write `likes:post9#0` ... `likes:post9#7` (pick the suffix
from a sequence or at random), and read all eight and add them up. Writes spread eight ways; reads cost eight
lookups. Only salt the keys you know are hot.
```text
before                         after salting into 4
likes:post9  -> s2  (6,000/s)   likes:post9#0 -> s0  1,500/s
likes:post9#1 -> s3  1,500/s
likes:post9#2 -> s1  1,500/s
likes:post9#3 -> s2  1,500/s
- **Hot spot**: a shard (or key) that takes far more than its share of the load, so adding shards does not help.

prompt: **Symptom first.** It is 09:05 on a Monday. The orders cluster pages: `shard-07 CPU > 95%`. The per-shard
dashboard shows the rest are quiet. Orders use a `bigint` identity column as the partition key, range
partitioned, 8 shards. What is the most likely cause?
options: Every new order gets the next id, so all inserts land in the last range: a time-ordered key on range partitioning
A celebrity customer is placing thousands of orders
The load balancer sends all traffic to shard-07
steps.explain: Growing ids plus range partitioning means the newest range takes all the writes. Hash the key (or partition by a high-cardinality key like `customer_id`) so new rows spread. Splitting shard-07 only moves the problem to the new last range.

steps.title: Which range owns the key?
prompt: Range partitioning keeps a sorted list of **exclusive upper bounds**. With bounds `{ 100, 200, 300 }` there
are four shards: shard 0 holds keys below 100, shard 1 holds `[100, 200)`, shard 2 `[200, 300)`, and shard 3
Write `int RangeShard(long key, long[] upperBounds)`. Keys may be negative (they go to shard 0).
hints: Walk the bounds in order and return the first index whose bound is greater than the key.
If no bound is greater, the key belongs to the last, open-ended shard: index `upperBounds.Length`.
template: Dojo.Eq("5 is in shard 0", 0, RangeShard(5, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("100 is the first key of shard 1 (bounds are exclusive)", 1, RangeShard(100, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("299 is in shard 2", 2, RangeShard(299, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("300 goes to the open-ended last shard", 3, RangeShard(300, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("a huge key goes to the last shard too", 3, RangeShard(9_000_000_000, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("negative keys go to shard 0", 0, RangeShard(-7, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("no bounds means one shard", 0, RangeShard(42, new long[0]));

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: seeing partitions and shards
steps.body: When load is uneven, first find out where a key lives and how much each partition holds. These are the commands for the stores you will meet most.

toolkit.what: PostgreSQL declarative partitioning: one logical table, several physical partitions on the same server. It is partitioning, not sharding across machines (extensions such as Citus spread partitions over nodes).
flags: rows go to a partition by the hash of the key
PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0)
toolkit.example: CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint, customer_id bigint, total numeric) PARTITION BY HASH (customer_id);
toolkit.when: a big table needs smaller indexes, faster vacuum, or cheap deletes of old ranges

toolkit.cmd: SELECT tableoid::regclass, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY 1
toolkit.what: Counts rows per partition in PostgreSQL: `tableoid` is the partition each row really lives in.
toolkit.example: SELECT tableoid::regclass AS part, count(*) FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
toolkit.when: checking that a hash partition key really spreads the rows

toolkit.what: In Cassandra the partitioner turns the partition key into a token on the ring; `token()` shows it, so you can see where rows sit.
flags: the Murmur3 token of the partition key
toolkit.example: SELECT token(user_id), user_id FROM shop.carts LIMIT 5;

toolkit.what: Prints the replicas (node addresses) that own one partition key. The fastest way to find the node behind a hot key.
flags: the partition key value, as text
toolkit.when: one node is hot and you suspect one key

toolkit.what: Every node in the Cassandra cluster with its state (UN = up, normal), load on disk and the share of the ring it owns.
flags: the percentage of data this node replicates
give a keyspace to get effective ownership for its replication

toolkit.what: Redis Cluster has 16,384 hash slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. A **hash tag** `{...}` makes only the part in braces count, so related keys share a slot (and can be used in one multi-key command).
flags: user:{user42}:cart and user:{user42}:orders land in the same slot

toolkit.what: Moves hash slots (and their keys) between Redis Cluster nodes while the cluster keeps serving.
toolkit.when: a new node joined, or one node holds too many hot slots

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it tells you.
pairs: which nodes hold this one partition key
each node's state, load and share of the ring
the Redis Cluster slot a key maps to
how many rows each PostgreSQL partition holds

steps.prompt: Hash-partition `orders` by customer into 4 partitions in PostgreSQL. Complete the first partition.
code: CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint, customer_id bigint, total numeric)
CREATE TABLE orders_p0 PARTITION OF orders
steps.explain: Each hash partition takes the rows whose hash of `customer_id`, mod `MODULUS`, equals `REMAINDER`. You need partitions for remainders 0 to 3, or inserts for the missing remainders fail.

steps.title: Find the hot shard, salt the hot key
prompt: Two helpers for the on-call runbook.
1. `List<int> HotShards(double[] writesPerSec, double factor)`: the indexes (in order) of shards whose writes are
**more than** `factor` times the average over all shards. With `{ 100, 100, 100, 700 }` the average is 250, so
with factor 2 only shard 3 (700 > 500) is hot.
2. `List<string> SaltedKeys(string key, int buckets)`: every salted row a reader must fetch, `key#0` up to
hints: `writesPerSec.Average()` gives the mean; compare each shard with `factor * average`.
template: Dojo.Eq("one hot shard", new List<int> { 3 }, HotShards(new double[] { 100, 100, 100, 700 }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("an even cluster has none", new List<int>(), HotShards(new double[] { 100, 110, 90, 100 }, 1.5));
Dojo.Eq("two hot shards, in order", new List<int> { 0, 1 }, HotShards(new double[] { 500, 500, 0, 0 }, 1.5));
Dojo.Eq("exactly factor x average is not hot", new List<int>(), HotShards(new double[] { 200, 100, 0 }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("an idle cluster has none", new List<int>(), HotShards(new double[] { 0, 0, 0 }, 2));
Dojo.Eq("no shards, no hot shards", new List<int>(), HotShards(new double[0], 2));
Dojo.Eq("one bucket is just one row", new List<string> { "k#0" }, SaltedKeys("k", 1));

steps.title: Build it: the hot shard
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *The hot shard*. Eight shards, range partitioned on time-ordered ids:
every write lands on the last one. Change the partitioning so the writes spread, then run the load test and
watch the per-shard utilisation even out. The board shows the exact goals.
steps.explain: Hash partitioning turns a growing key into an evenly spread one. You lose cheap range scans on that key, which is the trade-off to say out loud.
